---
title: "Quiz: fine-tuning strategies"
---

Short questions on how to fine-tune. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why should the new head get a larger learning rate than the pretrained layers?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where does each start?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The head starts from random weights and has everything to learn; the pretrained layers are already good and should move only a little. One rate for all is either too slow for the head or too fast for the backbone.
:::

---

**Q2.** What is catastrophic forgetting, and name two ways to limit it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the old task while training on the new one?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Training on the new task overwrites the weights the old task needed, so the network gets much worse at the old task (in the toy from 98 % to about a third). Freeze layers, use small or layer-wise rates, add a penalty pulling the weights towards the pretrained ones, mix old examples into the batches, or train only added parts (adapters, LoRA) and keep the original weights.
:::

---

**Q3.** A 1024 × 1024 weight matrix is changed with a rank-4 update $BA$. How many numbers are stored instead of the full change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$r(m + n)$ against $mn$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$4 \cdot 2048 = 8192$ instead of $1{,}048{,}576$: 0.8 %.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does LoRA start with $B = 0$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is $W_0 + BA$ at the start?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Then $BA = 0$ and the network starts exactly as the pretrained one; training only adds a change. ($A$ is random so that the gradient of $B$, which involves $A\mathbf x$, is not zero.)
:::

---

**Q5.** The singular values of a weight change are 5, 4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1 and smaller. Which rank would you choose for a low-rank update, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where is the knee?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rank 2: the first two singular values carry almost all of the change ($25 + 16 = 41$ of about $41.14$ in squared size; the relative error is about $\sqrt{0.14/41.14} \approx 6$ %); the rest is a small tail.
:::

---

**Q6.** You want to adapt SAM to outline your cells. Which part do you fine-tune first, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Heavy encoder, light decoder.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The light mask decoder: few weights (less overfitting with few annotated cells), the heavy encoder's embeddings can be computed once per image and stored, and the general image features of the encoder are kept.
:::
